claims.text: HfNbTaTiZr can be produced from mechanically alloyed powders using spark plasma sintering.
Systematically varying the relative percentages of Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr during powder blending, followed by SPS, can be used to study composition-dependent mechanical properties.
Changing the relative percentages of the constituent elements will systematically change the mechanical properties of HfNbTaTiZr.
The initial material consists of mechanically alloyed elemental Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr powders.
The initial HfNbTaTiZr powder mixture is equiatomic or near-equiatomic.
Low oxygen content is an important processing condition for obtaining promising SPS-processed HfNbTaTiZr material.
Holding SPS temperature, pressure, and atmosphere constant ensures that composition is the primary experimental variable.
Composition changes alter lattice distortion through atomic-size mismatch.
Composition changes alter phase stability in HfNbTaTiZr.
Hf and Ta are larger-atomic-radius constituents whose enrichment would increase lattice distortion.
Atomic-size differences create local lattice strain that affects dislocation mobility.
Changes in dislocation mobility alter the balance between hardness and ductility.
Increasing the Hf or Ta percentage will increase hardness through greater lattice distortion.
Increasing the Hf or Ta percentage may decrease ductility relative to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
An equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy processed by SPS under identical conditions is an appropriate baseline.
Composition changes of approximately 5–10 at.% or more are required to overcome the alloy's tolerance to compositional fluctuations and produce measurable effects.
Interaction effects among constituent elements may complicate direct correlations between composition and mechanical properties.
XRD, electron microscopy, hardness testing, and tensile testing can jointly evaluate phase, structural, and mechanical responses to composition changes.
